english.html: to kill him in the royal palace <sup class="mk" data-key="ſ">ſ</sup>. The like disaster befell Prompalus, who, being suborned by Ptolemy King of Egypt, Attalus King of Asia, Ariarathes King of Cappadocia and the people of Antioch to name and call himself Alexander, son of King Antiochus, and as such to demand the paternal kingdom from Demetrius, who had occupied Syria, undertook it, and fortune was so favourable to him that he vanquished him in the end, and killed Demetrius, and possessed peaceably the kingdom of Syria. True it is that afterwards the sweetness of this sceptre, the affluence of so many goods and honours, accompanied by a licence and liberty unchecked, corrupted him, and so captivated him to every kind of pleasure and lechery, that the very subjects of Antioch, by whom he had been made king, seeing him plunged into this abyss and confused labyrinth of vices, revolted, and gave themselves to the son of the late Demetrius, also called Demetrius, and afterwards Nicator: who thereupon vanquished this fine Prompalus, bastard king, and drove him into Arabia, where he was slain <sup class="mk" data-key="t">t</sup>. Archelaus likewise feigned to be the son of King Mithridates, which he so well persuaded Ptolemy king of Egypt that he gave him his daughter, and moreover afterwards made him his successor in the kingdom of Egypt: but in the end Gabinius vanquished him in the field of battle and killed him <sup class="mk" data-key="u">u</sup>. A like imposture was formerly practised, in the time of the Emperor Otho, by a harper calling himself Nero, because he took after him in the lineaments and features of the face, and in the height and bulk of the body: adding that when the rumour was spread at Rome that Nero had killed himself, another had been slain in his place: which was the cause that under the name of Nero he assembled several seditious men, with whom he was going into Syria and Egypt; whence, by the disfavour of the winds, he was carried to the island of Cythnus, among the Cyclades, where he used authority over the soldiers who came from the East, and constrained them to obey him: which being learned, almost all Asia was tottering, until Otho sent two galleys, by which the one in which this false Nero was was fought and vanquished, and this new Nero killed and his body sent to Rome <sup class="mk" data-key="x">x</sup>. notes.citation: Herodotus, book 3 (Thalia), chapters 61–79; Justin, book 1, chapter 9
notes.original: Herodote au iij. li. inſcript Thalia. Iuſtin au i. liure.
notes.gloss: The false Smerdis (Justin's Oropastes, "Mergis" being the dead brother in Justin), Prexaspes, Phaedima and Otanes, the cropped ears, and the seven conspirators.

notes.original: Appian Ale xandrin in Sy riacis.
notes.gloss: Alexander Balas, set up as son of Antiochus IV against Demetrius I Soter, then defeated by Demetrius II Nicator and killed in Arabia. Coras's Prompalus does not match any name in Appian.

notes.citation: Baptista Fulgosus (Battista Fregoso), Factorum dictorumque memorabilium libri IX, book 9, chapter 16
notes.original: Baptiſte Ful goſ. au liure ix. des dicts et faicts memora bles c. xvi.
notes.gloss: Archelaus, who claimed to be a son of Mithridates, married Berenice IV of Egypt and was killed by Gabinius in 55 BC; Fregoso's book is arranged after Valerius Maximus.

notes.citation: Suetonius, Life of Nero, chapter 57; Fregoso, the same chapter
notes.original: Sueton. en la vie de Neron, & Baptiſte Fulgoſe au lieu preallegué
notes.gloss: Suetonius records a false Nero twenty years after his death; the harper caught at Cythnus and his body sent to Rome are Tacitus, Histories 2.8–9, under Galba, as Fregoso probably had it.
